body: Summary: The caneept na]unaikulak is applied in many contexts in Eskimo life anel i s best glossed in English as: sign, symbol, marker, guide, characteristic or. most aptly, distinctive feature. Literally the ward me ans "i ts imp orlau t de-confuser" because, in action-oriented Inuit cultu re, it is the feature wh ich facihlates the initiation of a process of recognition and action, by cnding ignorance and confusion naJugiak end supplying the key to appropriate action and role behavior. Thus nalunaikulanga characterize not only sexes and spccies but also pl aces and people. enabling the Inuit to go ab out th e i r everyday lives of relating, cooperatinq, travelling, hunting and knowing. More recently, w ifh th e growth of individualism in Inuit commercial arts, individual arti s ts ' nalunaikutanga h av e been deve lopcd as aspects of style, subject matter, de te il or even m aterials us ed. title: Zusammenfassung (German Summary)
summary: Zusammenfassung: Der Begriff nahmaikutak (Sing.) wird im Leben der Eskimo (Inuit) in vielen Zus amm enh an qen angewandt.
body: Zusammenfassung: Der Begriff nahmaikutak (Sing.) wird im Leben der Eskimo (Inuit) in vielen Zus amm enh an qen angewandt. Im Deutschen ist er am besten durch Zeichen, Symbol, Markierung, Wegweiser, Leitfaden, kennzeichnendes und zugleich unterscheidendes Merkmal zu umschreiben; wörtlich übersetzt bedeutet der Begriff "wichtiger Entwirrer" . In der auf Handlung ausgerichteten Kultur der Inuit ist es diejenige Eigenschaft, die den Beginn eines Erkennungs- oder Handlungsprozesses erleichtert, indem sie Unkenntnis und Ver w ir ru nq (naJugiak) beendet und den Schlüssel zu angemessener Handlung und Rollenverhalten liefert. Auf diese Weise kennzeichnen naJunaikutanga (Pl.) nicht nur Geschlechter und Arten, sondern auch Orte und Personen, und ermöglichen den Inuit, der täqltchen Routine des Miteinanders, Zus amrnenw ir ken s , Re i s en s , Jagens und Erkennens nachzugehen. In j unq er e r Zeit sind mit dem Aufkommen des Individualismus in der kommerziellen Inuit-Kunst die naJUIwiku[anga einzelner KÜnstler in Fragen des Stils, der Thematik, der Detaildarstellung und sogar der We rk s toffe entwickelt worden. Während moderne Skulpturen im allgemeinen die traditionellen nalunaikulongCl des vorgegebenen Themas widerzuspiegeln vermögen - Reißzähne für Eisbären, Sennabel für Falken, amaulik-Kleidung für Frauen, Jagdwaffen für Männer usw. - , besteht doch die Gefahr, daß der Gehalt der zeitgenössischen Inuit-Kunstwerke herabsinkt zu einer Darstellung der nalunaikutanga der Weißen unter Verleugnung der besonderen, wenn auch nur noch verschwommen bekannten eigenen Vergangenheit.

title: Introduction
summary: In t rod u c t ion 1) Contemporary Inuit commercial arts have been with us for more than a quarter of a century and have been subject to extensive promotion, publicity and publication, we know very l…
body: In t rod u c t ion 1) Contemporary Inuit commercial arts have been with us for more than a quarter of a century and have been subject to extensive promotion, publicity and publication, we know very little about the mental activity or conceptual categories of those thousands of well-known Inuit art ists who have produced it. This essay is an attempt to describe one concept, that of nalunaikutanga, or "distinctive feature", which runs through the whole of Inuit culture and art 2). The meaning and importance of this concept is best understood not only by dissecting the compound word itself into its component morphemes but also by examining the contexts in which it is used both within and beyond the realm of what we call .thc arts" .

title: Semantic Structure
summary: The word nalunaikutanga ") is heard in many spheres of Eskimo life with the qross semantic content which may be glossed in English as: sign, symbol, marker, guide, characteristic, or, perhaps best, d…
body:
The word nalunaikutanga ") is heard in many spheres of Eskimo life with the qross semantic content which may be glossed in English as: sign, symbol, marker, guide, characteristic, or, perhaps best, distinctive feature. Literally the word me ans "its important de-confuser" which may be derived from the (in reverse order) -nga (= its) -kuta- (= great, remarkable, important) -i- (= negative, privative) -ria- (= causes or

makes to do or feel) nalu (= confused, ignorant), The wo rrl is always found in the form ending in -nga (third person possessive) far it is always a feature oi something o r somebody. Putting the word back together less than literally one might translate it to mean "its important thing by which one ceases to be confused about it ", or "that which enables one to recognize it ". In the Inuit plan for purposive action, which I have demonstrated elsewhere applies as much to carving sr ulptures, as to sexual or hunting activity (Graburn 1974; 1976). there comes a point at which generalized or scarchinq activity, qiniikpul«, gives way to purposive or directed activity phuisuk.puk, paralleling the English distinction between hunt for and hunt down. It is the nafunaikutanga which enables the actor to recognize the quarry or goal which is in sight or within reach at last. In the plan for purposive action Inuit will start by saying nafulukpunga, I am confused or dori't know exactly what to do, followed by "Ah", nalunangituk, it is no longer confusing, or even, qcwjimavunga, I know, in the sense that I recognize something quite familiar. Though the characteristic feature by which something or someone is recognized is olten elear, many Inuit are not introspective enough to be able to verbalize it immediately in most cases. Just as when we are asked "Ho w do you know sc-arid-so when you sce him?" we hesitate or we are unable to reply directly, so the Inuit are olten unaware of the spr.cific signs or the gestalt by which they know something. Thus at present it is not possible to state elearly whether nalunaikutanga as a elass are conscious or unconscious or whether they are linked to wh at they represent in an essential or arbitrary way (as we sometimes try to distinguish between sign and syrnbol).

title: The Context of Recognition
summary: Let us now consider the range of applications of the concept nalwwilwtanga starting with the widest and most natural and ending wih the most human and specific.
body:
Let us now consider the range of applications of the concept nalwwilwtanga starting with the widest and most natural and ending wih the most human and specific. In the relatively featureless land of the Inuit pI aces are recognized by specific physical features, e. g. Lake Harbour is called kimmirut, "[like a] hcel", because of a rock Iormation that would be recognized by anyone boating or sIedding into the inlet from afar. Sometimes places or routes are recognized more by "relationships: relationships between, say, contour, type of snow, wind, sult air, ice crack" (Carpenter, Varley & Flaherty 1959; Carpenter 1973: 21'j) A consideration of Inuit toponymy (Müller-Wille 1975) revcals some of these noted features. But olten they are not marked in nature

at all, and the Inuit put up their own markers all over the countryside by building characteristic piles of stones inukeuk (= imitation person) in visible places. (Photo. 1.). Th e species of the natural world are also known and recognized by their distinctive features, nutunuikuuuu;a, though understandably, only a minority of the Inuit are able to state firmly what they are for few wear the gramm ar of their conceptual world "on their sleeve" - however on discussion of particular natunailcuicuiqa Inuit of ten glow with realization and pleasure at making conscious the guides to many of their actions. The following list will show that tuilunaik utünqa of species are neither solely their v isibly most characteristic feature nor are they necessarily their behaviorally strangest point, but generally they are a synthesis of the two - the visible features which suggest their behavioral propensities. For instance for nanuk, the polar bear, natunoikutanqa include the incisors tulluriak. and the claws kuk.i, (Photo. 2.) suggesting the b e ar's striking power, as weIl as its tongue oqak: which is portrayed in some sculptural examples. The polar be ars only serious opponent aiv itk the walrus is known mainly by its tusks tuqatc, as weil as its moustaches umik (Photo, 3.) Caribou are known by their antlers, najjuk and their hooves kuki. These leave very distinctive footprints tumil in the snow as do all land animals. Among the birds (lingmink) the birds of prey arouse interest and admiration far beyond their edibility, stemming from their paralleling male Inuit activities. Perhaps the owls, ulspil: are the most distinctive, and their nulutiaikuuuiqa along w.th those of other birds of prey are the hooked beak sigguk and the striking claws kuk.i used for killing. The owl is also known by its raund and foreward facing eyes, suggestive of a human oxpression. Other birds may be known by their colors, e. g. the raven lulugak by its black cirnitak. feathers (Photo, 4), and the seagull naujoi: by their white qokurkuik. It might be noted that traditional Inuit mythology go es to some length to explain the colors of these birds as weil as the other features of the species under discussion. Canutla geese nirlit l: were traditionally known by their neck markinqs (and calls 5) but nowadays they are additionally known by the strange rings that encircle their legs (Photo, 5.). The edible sea mammals all have their d.stinctivc Ieutures. the square flipper seal its beard or Ulnik, just as the narwhal aqlünquak exhibi ts its tusk tuqak., the beluga qilaluqal: its white sk.n makuik: and the common seal natsiq its inquisitive face and the rings on its pelt. One could go on almost cn dlcssl y to mention the colors and actions of fish, the smaller mammals and birds, and all other natural beings, edible, useful or otherwise, which

populate the Inuit world. Even temporal dimensions such as the seasons have then distinctive markers: e. g. spring is heralded by the eruption of the permafrost right through ice and snow covering shallows and mudflats, known as upingaksClksiutik. Most important of all are people, other Inuit, and where nature is lacking (e. g. in facial hair) or weil covered up, artificial means are selected for marking age and sex making it easy to embark upon appropriate role behavior. Even from babyhood, boys and girls whose clothes are otherwise identical wear adult style boots whose applique stripes run appropriately up and down for boys and round in a circle for girls. Even after puberty girls without children may continue to wear "mens" clothing, but in traditional days, their prominant face tatooing tutinit (Photo. 6) marked them as post menarche an d available. Even more striking was the difference between adult men's and worneu's parkas, the latter with its sweeping front and rear tail s aqu and large back pouch Cl111ClUti for carrying a child. Full or empty the bowl-like ovoid shape of the opening of the amauti is characteristically female (Photo. 17.), and is perhaps the prime nolutiaikiitanoa of women in both art and life. The relative shapes of mcns and wornen's parkas are emphasized by the lines paralleling the edges made from contrasting colored caribou skin, also frequently represented in Inuit two and three dimensional arts (Photo. 8). Other features diagnostic of adult men and WOm811 include the knives, harpoons an d kajaks of the former, arid of women, hairstyle, soapstone lamps qullik, the ulu semi-lunar knife (see Photo. 17). Sometimes individual women marle skin parkas and boots for themselves and their families with very characteristic decorative patterns IClksa·k in such a way that they became individual ntüunaikuuuiqc: within the social group (Photo. 8) in the same way that individualism later entered commercial Inuit arts. Regional differences were less important than sex and age differences. However, characteristic parka lengths and contours and particularly, male and female hood peaks, served to distinguish one group from another. These regional neighbour {nunaqatiqit} nnlunaihutonqa used to be important in the days when strangers were viewed with suspicion and might be subject to attack unless recognized from a distance. Beyond the demarcation of region, age an d sex, particular individuals used to b e known (and called) by certain visual or behavioral characteristics that set them apart from the group. Names (atiit] ar e a kind of nolunuikutonqa ii they t elet to some obcervable duirneterist ic otherwise names are more arbitrary (having been given at birth) and are no help in recognition. Individuals may stand out and be named after unique features, such as Elijah "Scar" , or by their unusual stature or girth. These may be marked by suffixes added onto common names, a laugh, a limp, a squint, or whatever. Even the anthropologist is quickly so named in one settlement I was dubbed the big red one - because of a large red down parka that I (alone) wore. au.pulukiulul: -

title: Nalunaikutanga in Contemporary Inuit Arts
summary: Nalunaikutanga enter into the process of Inuit arts in two ways.
body:
Nalunaikutanga enter into the process of Inuit arts in two ways. Most fundamentally

the work of art itself should exhibit the overt features of the subject portrayed in a way that is satisfactory to the reference group of the artist: the reference groups of the vast majority of the artists are other Inuit, thus the same kinds of nCllunaikulClngCl that we have discussed above for the natural world appear in the majority of the two and three dimensional arts of the Inuit 6). That is how I was able to illustrate the

first part of this paper from the In uits own art works. Not all nalwwikulanga are equally amenable to portrayal and those most suitable to the particular medium are those included. Increasingly since the incipient commercialism of the early 1950s it is not only whal the sculptor or print maker has portrayed, but who did it that has mattered; the rewards of commercial art are given to individuals and the market system encourages individual styles within regional styles (Carpenter 1973; Graburn 1976). The particular ways in which artists choose to express their individuality (consciously or unco nsciously) vary immensely, as we shall see. The most obvious and widespread form of individual artistic nalunaikulanga is the siqnaturc (Photo. 9.). and Inuit have put these on their art works with and without explicit instruction since the late 1950s. (Before this time one had to recognize works of art on the b asi s of other formal features described below). However it is features other than the ac tu al name which are still ordinarily used by Inuit today in recognizing the works of their neighbours, but not all pay particular attention to this as not all are so competitive or self-confident (See Graburn 1974). The famous Pautak of Cape Dorset has gone one step further than most, it is said, in putting the signature an the side of his sculptures where it can be seen rather than on the base where it is usually hidden. There is not the time here to describe all the various ways artists express their individuality, so only some of the better known examples will be illustrated. Formal elements may characterize the works of particular artists, such as the lobe-like conncctedness of Qirnuajuak's prints, the child-like scratchiness of Paa's drawings, or the perfeetion of faithfulness to naturalistic detail in the prints of Kananginak and the sculptures of Siirkjuk (Photo. 10) and Qupirgualuk, but these are not always considered by the Inuit to be the noluncukutcnqa of an individual's work. More impo rtantly it is the choice and treatment of subject matter which the Inuit look for: this is expressed in two ways. Some artists tend to include in their scenes and sculptures small details which are absent in the works of others: such "arbitrary" nalunaikulanga include the bootlaces ungiruli delicately incised on the otherwise massive carvings of Leviraluk (Photo. 11) or Joe Talirunilik's inclusion of horned owls siutilik and hares ugalirk in his vigorous hunting scenes (Photo. 12). The carvings and prints of his neighbour Leah Qumaluk are always tinged w ith fear and mystery and her prints often show overt violence. More than the details it is the central theme of subject matter itself which characterizes the work of certain artists, This is partly because artists become adept at certain scenes or figures an d partly because these subjects are frequently on their minds, for reasons which may stem from their personality and life experiences. Leviraluk usually portrays burly successful hunters, with their game and weapons (see Photo. 11 above). Ainalik of Ivujuvik used to like to show a man sitting on a walrus head. The late Niviaksi, it is said, constantly thought about and carved polar bears, until he met his death at the hands (or paws) of one. Davidialuk of Povungnituk most frequently portrays scenes from Inuit mythology (Photo. 13). whereas his step-son Eli Sallualuk Qirnuajuak has increasingly been associated with non-traditional scenes of imaginative man-animal distortions, lakusurngncliluk (Photo 14.) (Trafford, 1968). Qakjurakjuk of Cape Dorset is known for her owls, as is the better known Qirnuajuak. Aisaki of Sugluk is famous for his man-and-Iarge animal themes (photo 15) but this is a nalunaikulanga of not just an individual but of his whole family, including his brother Paulasi, and his cousins Qupak and Kululak. Papi-kutak makes very mi n iatu re scenes where his brother-in-Iaw Paulasikutak created boldly conceived naturalistic men and women (Photo. 16), Limite tio ns of subject matter have from time to time characterized the arts of whole settle9

ments and regions, such as the large-animals-fighting which first came from Wakeham Bay, and the classic working-women emerged from Ivujivik arid Sugluk (Photo. 17) in the 1950s and 1960s. With the increasing quantities of sculptures pro duced and their greater economic importance, individualism has more recently been emphasized as against regional styles. The type of rock used in sculptures is sometimes recognized as the nalunaikunlanga of individuals, for instance the extremely hard field stone that only Qakak attacks is the mark of his works (Photo. 18) whereas the soft imported talc stone that old and weak people use is considered the mark of women, and hence unmanly men. The type of stone is, however, more commonly the natunaikuuuica of a region, Ior the available local stones vary immensely, and usually there are only two or three kinds found in each area. Thus most Inuit would use the hardness, grain, striations and other qualities of the material to identify sculptures from other regions where they rarely have a knowledge of individual styles of people who live in those places t nunaqatujiinqitutj. We have already seen some of the characteristic sto n es from various areas, such as the light and mid-green serpentine of Cape Derset. the browny green of Lake Harbour, the blue-grey of Repulse Bay, the striped slate from Belcher Is. and Great Whale River (Photo. 9), and the very even coloured soft and malleable greyblack stone from Povungnituk and Port Harrison (see Photos. 5, 6, 11, etc.). The types of stone are also markers of some kind of "authenficity" to the art market nowadays arid when the Government moves to ship up North replacement of the local stone which has already run out in many areas.

title: Discussion and Conclusions
summary: The Central Canadian Inuit are "interested not in scenery but in action" (Carpenter, 1973: 41).
body:
The Central Canadian Inuit are "interested not in scenery but in action" (Carpenter, 1973: 41). What counts is not their possession or contemplation of people or objects but their relations and actions to them. Thus the nalunailwtanga are the key features in aseries af actions which either (i) enable the Inuit to know and hence relate, particularly to other people, and/or (ii) to know and account for the relationships that others have with each other, e. g. the beaks and claws of birds of prey arid the teeth and tusks of bears and walruses. Carpen ters assertions (1959, 1973) that Inuit commercial arts are totally removed from traditional (ivory) carving or from the concepts of Inuit life, have so far proven false as we have shown that (i) the nalunaikutcuuja of traditional life and myth are the key to the art works of most contemporary Inuit and (ii) the way the Inuit go about their new arts is built upon the traditional base plan of searchlrecognition followed by action! result. Even Carpenter's description of near tradition al ivory carvings Art to the Eskimo (Aivilik) is an act, not an object; a ritual, not apossession , , , Art to them is a transitory act, a relationship. They are more interested in the creative activity than in the product of that activity, . , Once carved ... it may be passed from hand to hand, then dropped indifferently .. , or simply lost,. ." (Carpenter 1973: 75, 63, 75; Carpenter, Varley & Flaherty 1959: no pagination), aptly describes the Inuit involvement with their contamporarv arts. Wh at they do is to enjoy the process of creation arid look forward to the end result, but they still do not keep or display their carvings or drawings - they give them away, trade them and never see them again. Only those very few more acculturated office employees decorate their everyday environments with Eskimo art. Paa never hung his own art works in his house, but when a Toronto calendar company sent him framed r eproductions of his own prints he hung them proudly next to his Centennial Medal as something prestigeful, coming from the outside.

\Vhen an Eskimo sets out to carve stone or to draw on paper (for an eventual print) he (or she) starts with an air of puzzlement nalulukpuk. Rarely does he start with subject or object in mind. He turns the stone over and over, chips away at certain parts with aseries of ideas, ishuma, flash.nq through his mind. He is looking Ior gross form, for ability of the particular rock to carry an image (or of paper to contain one) and suddenly he can attack the rock (or the surface) with the complete plan in mind. He has its essential nalunaikutanga in mind, and often starts to sketch or to shape these first, or at least prepare to fit them into the medium. Generalized action turns into purposive action, and this action is wh at provides pleasure and satisfaction. Let me conclude by raising th o suggestion that there is the possibility that Inuit arts may be moving from a rich expression of life as it is lived to a fossilized portrayal of an idealized past. As I have po in ted out elsewhere (Graburn 1975) the content of the arts which portrayed an experienced way of life in the early 1950s has given way to a memory art concerning things that the present day Inuit and Qallunat, white people, think of as admired features of the traditional Inuit way of life. If the art form came t.o be a standard set of symbols th at no longer relate to life and action it would be ironic that the features of the art would consist of those niiuuunkutonqa which the white art market h as imposed on the Inuit artists. Thus either the essential purpose of the nalunaikutanga would become irrelevant to the Inuit themselves, or they would have learned to look at themselves and th eir past "through the eyes of" white culture.

title: Polar Bear · nanuk
summary: The polar bear (nanuk) is recognized by its incisors (tulluriak) and claws (kuki), suggesting its striking power, as well as its tongue (oqak).
body: For nanuk, the polar bear, the nalunaikutanga include the incisors (tulluriak) and the claws (kuki) — features that suggest the bear's striking power — as well as its tongue (oqak), which is portrayed in some sculptural examples. The polar bear is the most distinctive of the land predators in Inuit art and culture.

title: Walrus · aivik
summary: The walrus (aivik), the polar bear's only serious opponent, is known mainly by its tusks (tugak) and its moustaches (umik).
body: The polar bear's only serious opponent, the walrus (aivik), is known mainly by its tusks (tugak), as well as its moustaches (umik). The tusks are the dominant recognition-feature carried over into carved and printed depictions.

title: Caribou · tuktu
summary: Caribou are known by their antlers (najjuk) and their hooves (kuki), which leave very distinctive footprints (tumit) in the snow.
body: Caribou are known by their antlers (najjuk) and their hooves (kuki). Like all land animals, they leave very distinctive footprints (tumit) in the snow — themselves a nalunaikutanga that allows a creature to be recognized in its absence, by the trace it leaves.

title: Owl · uppik
summary: The owl (uppik) is perhaps the most distinctive bird of prey, known by its hooked beak (sigguk), striking claws (kuki), and round, forward-facing eyes.
body: Among the birds of prey — admired for paralleling male Inuit activities — the owls (uppik) are perhaps the most distinctive. Their nalunaikutanga, shared with other raptors, are the hooked beak (sigguk) and the striking claws (kuki) used for killing. The owl is also known by its round, forward-facing eyes, suggestive of a human expression.

title: Raven · tulugak
summary: The raven (tulugak) is known by its black feathers; traditional Inuit mythology takes pains to explain the colours of such birds.
body: Some birds are known by their colours: the raven (tulugak) by its black feathers, and the seagull (nauja) by its white. Traditional Inuit mythology goes to some length to explain the colours of these birds as well as the other distinctive features of the species under discussion.

title: Canada Goose · nirlik
summary: Canada geese (nirlit) were traditionally known by their neck markings and calls, and nowadays additionally by the rings that encircle their legs.
body: Canada geese (nirlit) were traditionally recognized by their neck markings and by their calls. Nowadays they are additionally known by the strange rings that encircle their legs — a modern nalunaikutanga added by banding, layered over the traditional ones.

title: Narwhal · aglunguaq
summary: The narwhal (aglunguaq) exhibits its tusk (tugak) as its prime distinctive feature.
body: Among the edible sea mammals, each has its distinctive feature. The narwhal (aglunguaq) exhibits its tusk (tugak), the single spiralled feature by which it is unmistakably recognized.

title: Beluga · qilaluga
summary: The beluga (qilaluga) is known by its white skin (makuik).
body: The beluga whale (qilaluga) is recognized by its white skin (makuik) — its colour serving, as with the raven and seagull, as the immediate sign by which it is told apart from other sea mammals.

title: Common Seal · natsiq
summary: The common seal (natsiq) is known by its inquisitive face and the rings on its pelt; the square-flipper seal by its beard.
body: The edible sea mammals all have their distinctive features. The common seal (natsiq) is known by its inquisitive face and the rings on its pelt, while the square-flipper seal is recognized by its beard (ujjuk). These features are the ones most amenable to portrayal in carving and print.

title: Women · the amauti
summary: The bowl-like ovoid opening of the amauti — the woman's parka with its large back pouch for carrying a child — is perhaps the prime distinctive feature of women in both art and life.
body: Where nature is lacking or covered up, artificial means mark age and sex. The most striking is the difference between men's and women's parkas: the woman's, with its sweeping front and rear tails (saqu) and its large back pouch (amauti) for carrying a child. Full or empty, the bowl-like ovoid shape of the amauti's opening is characteristically female, and is perhaps the prime nalunaikutanga of women in both art and life. Further female markers include the semi-lunar ulu knife, the soapstone lamp (qullik), hairstyle, and the prominent face tattoos (tunnit) that traditionally marked a girl as post-menarche.

title: Men · weapons & the kayak
summary: Adult men are recognized by their knives, harpoons, and kayaks — the hunting weapons that distinguish male role and activity.
body: Features diagnostic of adult men include the knives, harpoons, and kayaks of the hunter. As the work of art should exhibit the overt features of its subject, these hunting weapons recur throughout the two- and three-dimensional arts as the nalunaikutanga of men, paralleling male Inuit activity.

title: Inuksuk · the stone marker
summary: Where the land bears no natural markers, the Inuit build characteristic piles of stones — inuksuk, 'imitation person' — in visible places to mark routes and places.
body: In the relatively featureless land of the Inuit, places are recognized by specific physical features, but often these are not marked in nature at all. So the Inuit put up their own markers across the countryside by building characteristic piles of stones — inuksuk, literally 'imitation person' — in visible places. The inuksuk is a built nalunaikutanga: a sign deliberately raised so that a place or route can be recognized from afar.

title: Names · atiit
summary: Names (atiit) act as distinctive features when they refer to an observable characteristic — a scar, stature, a limp, a squint — though birth-names are otherwise arbitrary.
body: Particular individuals used to be known and called by visual or behavioral characteristics that set them apart. Names (atiit) are a kind of nalunaikutanga when they refer to some observable characteristic; otherwise, names given at birth are arbitrary and no help in recognition. Individuals may be named after unique features — Elijah 'Scar', or for unusual stature or girth — marked by suffixes added to common names: a laugh, a limp, a squint. Even the visiting anthropologist was quickly named for the large red parka he alone wore.

title: The Artist's Signature
summary: Since the late 1950s the signature is the most obvious and widespread form of individual artistic nalunaikutanga, marking who made a work rather than only what it depicts.
body: Nalunaikutanga enter Inuit art in two ways: the work must show the overt features of its subject, and the work increasingly shows the distinctive mark of its maker. The most obvious and widespread form of individual artistic nalunaikutanga is the signature, applied to art works since the late 1950s. The famous Pautak of Cape Dorset went one step further, placing his signature on the side of his sculptures where it can be seen, rather than hidden on the base.
